A Response object, with its own attributes and methods for the status code, body, headers, and more
Nothing — it only prints the result to the console

questions.explain: requests.get() returns a Response object. You then read its status_code, text, headers, or call .json() to get specific information out of it.

questions.explain: status_code is a plain integer representing the HTTP status returned by the server — 200 for success, 404 for not found, and so on (covered fully in Lesson 24).

questions.q: What is the difference between `response.text` and `response.json()`?
options: response.text returns the raw body as a string; response.json() parses that body as JSON and returns a Python dict or list
They are identical in every case
response.json() only works on GET requests, never POST
response.text requires an internet connection but response.json() does not
questions.explain: response.text gives the unparsed body as a plain string, useful for any content type. response.json() additionally parses that string as JSON, handing you a ready-to-use dict or list.

questions.q: Why did `requests` become the standard third-party HTTP library instead of everyone using Python's built-in `urllib`?
options: urllib was removed from Python entirely
requests is illegal to use outside the United States
requests wraps the complexity of urllib behind a small, readable API, making common tasks much simpler to write
urllib cannot make HTTP requests at all
questions.explain: Python's built-in urllib can make HTTP requests, but it requires significantly more boilerplate for common tasks. requests became the ecosystem standard by making the common case (GET, POST, reading JSON) simple.

questions.q: Why is understanding `requests` directly useful even if you mostly plan to use a provider SDK like `openai` or `anthropic`?
options: Provider SDKs don't use HTTP at all, so there's no connection
SDKs are built on top of an HTTP library like requests internally, so understanding requests demystifies what the SDK is actually doing
requests is required to install any SDK
It isn't useful; SDK users never need to know this
questions.explain: Every provider SDK ultimately sends HTTP requests under the hood. Learning requests directly gives you a mental model for what an SDK call is actually doing on the network, which makes its behavior (including errors) far less mysterious.
